# Changes in US Skilled Nursing Facility Capacity following the Covid-19 Pandemic

**Authors:** Brian E. McGarry; Andrew D. Wilcock; Ashvin D. Gandhi; David C. Grabowski; Fangli Geng; Michael L. Barnett

**Affiliations:** 1University of Rochester, Rochester, NY | 2Brown School of Public Health, Providence, RI | 3University of California Los Angeles | 4Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts

## Abstract

Skilled nursing facilities (SNF) are the primary provider of institutional post-acute care. Following the Covid-19 pandemic, there are reports of SNFs reducing their capacity, affecting access to care and disrupting hospital discharges yet little empirical evidence exists.

Describe changes in SNF capacity after 2020 and assess whether changes were associated with staffing shortages and hospital discharge outcomes.

Descriptive analyses characterized trends in SNF capacity from 2018-2024. Data sources included the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Payroll-Based Journal and hospital data. County-level regression analyses examined the association between changes in SNF capacity and the frequency of SNF staffing shortages. Hospital-level regressions examined the association between changes in nearby SNF capacity and discharge outcomes.

SNF licensed bed count, estimated operating capacity, and available capacity (i.e., difference between operating capacity and census). Secondary outcomes included SNF staffing shortages, mean hospital length of stay, share of hospital admissions lasting ≥28 days, and the median distance traveled to admitting SNFs.

From 2019 to 2024, the number of licensed SNF beds declined modestly, while operating capacity declined by 5.0%. There was significant geographic variation—1 in 4 counties experienced capacity declines of 15.1% or more, with the largest declines being more common among rural counties. SNF capacity declines were larger in counties with more frequent reports of SNF staffing shortages—a 1 percentage point (pp) decline in county SNF capacity was associated with a 0.20pp increase (95%CI: 0.11,0.29) in the frequency of reported shortages. Additionally, hospitals that experienced larger declines in nearby SNF capacity experienced greater increases in mean length of stay, share of stays lasting ≥28 days, and median distance traveled to admitting SNFs.

Although licensed SNF bed counts declined modestly following the pandemic, actual operating capacity declines were larger, potentially because of staffing shortages. Greater loss of SNF capacity was associated with longer hospital stays and increased travel distances to SNFs, suggesting that declines in operating capacity may be impairing access to care.

The Covid-19 pandemic severely disrupted the nursing home, or skilled nursing facility (SNF), industry in several ways, including a historic decline in workforce and straining facility operations.1–4 As many as 35% of SNFs reported staffing shortages in a given week in 2022, with large increases in the use of costly overtime hours and agency staff to compensate.5–7 These staffing and resulting financial challenges may be forcing SNFs to close or scale back their operations.8,9 Although closures did not spike in 2020 or 2021,10 an industry report indicated that by 2024, 46% of SNFs were limiting new admissions and 20% had closed entire units due to staffing shortages.11

Declines in SNF capacity (i.e., the maximum number of patients they are able to safely care for at a point in time) may have important implications for the broader health care system. SNFs are a critical source of post-acute care for hospitalized older adults, with nearly 1 in 5 Medicare hospitalizations being discharged to a SNF.12 A loss of available SNF beds due to staffing shortages or other causes may therefore impede hospitals’ ability to discharge clinically stable patients in need of rehabilitation, resulting in hospital bottlenecks. Though national evidence is lacking, numerous media reports have suggested this scenario is playing out across multiple markets in the US.11,13–18 Several state hospital association reports corroborate these stories of disrupted patients flows, and a lack of available SNF capacity is consistently reported as a primary cause.14,19,20

Despite the potential importance of a shrinking SNF market for the health system at large, little empirical evidence exists about recent trends in SNF capacity. A key limitation to generating this evidence is that typical metrics for SNF capacity may provide an incomplete or even misleading picture. For example, a standard measure for quantifying capacity is facility occupancy, calculated as the count of individuals in a SNF divided by the SNF’s number of licensed beds. Occupancy loses value as a capacity measure if SNFs reduce the number of beds in operation, as observed after the pandemic, without formally reducing the number of bed licenses they hold. With fewer beds in “real world” use but no change in licensed beds, occupancy rates could indicate significant excess capacity, when the opposite is true. Indeed, SNF occupancy rates in 2024 were 5% lower than in 2019 (suggesting an increase in capacity),21 even though there is scarce evidence that SNF capacity has improved in real terms.

In this analysis, we aim to fill the evidence gap in understanding SNF capacity by measuring recent changes in both licensed bed counts and a novel measure of “operating capacity,” which we estimate via facilities’ recent maximum patient census, following the start of the Covid-19 pandemic. Additionally, we examine the extent to which changes in SNF capacity were correlated with the frequency of reported nursing home staffing shortages and changes in hospital discharge outcomes that could be affected by impaired access to SNF care.

## Methods

### Data

The primary data source for this study was the 2018-2024 Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Payroll-Based Journal (PBJ) data.22 These data contain daily information on staffing hours and patient census for all Medicare- and Medicaid-certified SNFs. Due to the disruption caused by the initial wave of the Covid-19 pandemic, reporting to PBJ was made optional for the first quarter of 2020, resulting in about 20% of SNFs missing data for this quarter. We excluded this quarter from analyses as a result. We merged these data with information on licensed bed counts and other facility characteristics, obtained from the CMS Provider Information file.23

Information on SNF staffing shortages and Covid-19 case rates was obtained from the CMS Covid-19 Nursing Home Database which contained data submitted by nursing homes through the National Healthcare Safety Network.24 Starting in May of 2020, nursing homes were required to submit Covid-related information to this database on a weekly basis. Through the first quarter of 2023, the weekly survey required nursing homes to report whether they had, in the prior week, experienced staffing shortages in the following categories: 1) aides, 2) nurses, 3) clinical staff, and 4) other staff.

Information on hospital-related outcomes were obtained from the 2019-2022 Medicare Provider Analysis and Review File (MedPAR), the most recent data available to our study team. These data contain detailed information on all Medicare Part A hospital and SNF stays, as well as 90% of all Medicare Advantage hospitalizations.25 We paired these data with the Minimum Data Set v3.0 (MDS), which contains assessment information for virtually all SNF residents at regularly scheduled intervals. Finally, we obtained geographic information, such as urban/rural status, population age, and population poverty level, at the county level from Area Health Resources File,26 and county Covid burden from the NYTimes Covid-19 database.27

### SNF Capacity Measures

#### Licensed Bed Count and SNF Census:

For each day in our sample, we calculated the total number of licensed beds as the sum of bed licenses for all nursing homes who had a resident census of at least one patient in PBJ. Similarly, we calculated daily census totals by summing reported census counts across all US SNFs.

#### Operating Capacity:

Although facilities typically have a fixed number of certified beds, the availability of operational resources, such as direct care staff, administrators, therapists, and equipment, can further limit the number of residents the facility can accommodate. We infer facilities’ current “operating capacity” as the highest occupancy accommodated by a SNF over the prior 60 days.28,29 Intuitively, this approach assumes that the maximum recent census reasonably approximates the maximum number of residents the facility is capable of caring for based on current resource constraints. In sensitivity analyses, we examined the implications of shorter and longer look-back periods to ascertain the maximum patient census (eAppendix 2.1)

#### Estimated Open Beds:

The number of open beds at a nursing home is the difference between the operating capacity and census, representing the number of additional patients the facility could accommodate. Especially when aggregating across facilities in a region or the nation, available capacity provides a useful measure of “slack” in the SNF system that can be accessed by new patients in need of SNF care (eAppendix 2.2).

### SNF Staffing Shortage Measure

Staffing shortages were defined weekly at the SNF level as a binary measure that was equal to 1 if the facility self-reported a shortage in any staffing category (i.e., aides, nurses, clinical, and other staff). Facility-level shortages were aggregated to the county level using a weighted count of facilities within the county that reported a shortage in that week where the weights were defined by the bed size of the facility. This measure indicates the number of beds in each week that were experiencing a staffing shortage. In eAppendix 2.3, we examine how results vary when looking at specific categories of staff shortages (e.g., nurses vs. clinical staff).

### Hospital Measures

#### Hospital Length of Stay:

Hospital length of stay was measured for all Medicare admissions to short-stay acute care hospitals with at least 100 beds, excluding admissions coming directly from a SNF (as identified by having an MDS record that overlapped or ended within the 7 days preceding the hospital admission) and admissions related to Covid-19 (as identified by the presence of ICD-10 code U0.71 in any of the MedPAR diagnosis fields). Patients admitted to the hospital from a SNF were excluded because these patients may be guaranteed a spot at their prior SNF due to state bed hold policies or may have strong preferences use their prior SNF that make them less sensitive to region-level capacity.30 Covid-related admissions were excluded to ensure that changes in observed length of stay were not the result of changes in patient severity due to Covid-19.

Hospital length of stay was used to identify extended hospital stays, defined as those lasting 28 days or more. Such stays represented roughly the 99th percentile of all hospital lengths of stay in the data. Changes in the frequency of these outlier stays may provide an indicator of severely delayed discharges that are related to an inability to find a SNF placement.

#### Distance to Admitting SNF:

For the subgroup of hospitalizations that were eventually discharged to a SNF (i.e., hospital discharges with a corresponding MDS admission record within 7 days of a hospital discharge date), we calculated the distance between the centroid of the patient’s 5-digit ZIP code of residence and the admitting SNF. We summarized distance traveled at the hospital-year level using the median to account for the right-skewed distribution of this measure.

### Additional Measures

The AHRF and NYTimes Covid-19 datasets were used to construct measures describing counties. These measures included size of the population in the county, the share of the population age 75 and older, the racial/ethnic composition of the population, median household income, the share of the population with any college education, and the county’s Covid burden measured as the total Covid-19 cases reported throughout the pandemic per 100,000 population.

To characterize hospital use patterns over the study period, we calculated annual hospital volume (measured by as the total number of admissions meeting our study inclusion criteria) for each hospital year and predicted length of stay. Predicted length of stay served as a measure of patient case-mix and was estimated using a patient-level linear regression prediction model on observable characteristics from the hospital stay (see eAppendix 1 for details).

### Hospital-SNF Catchment Area

SNFs within a given hospital’s catchment area were defined as an SNF located within the hospital’s Hospital Referrral Region (HRR). These geographic areas have been shown to accurately capture hospital patient populations based on their residence, and prior research has demonstrated a strong preferences for patients to receive care from SNFs located close to their home.31–33

### Analytic Approach

Daily estimates of SNF capacity were calculated and rolling 30-day averages were used to graphically examine trends. Capacity measures were also summarized at the annual level and relative annual changes in capacity were calculated for the post-Covid years compared to 2019, the last full year prior to the start of the pandemic. Finally, annual capacity measures were aggregated to the county level to explore geographic variation in SNF capacity.

We examined the relationship between county-level changes in SNF capacity and the frequency of reported SNF staffing shortages using a linear regression model where the outcome was the share of county SNF bed-weeks with a reported staffing shortage and the independent variable was the annual relative change in SNF capacity in the county. For these analyses, we highlight the estimated relationship in 2022, the last full year of SNF staff shortage data available, and control for County Covid-19 case rates in 2022.

To examine the relationship between changes in SNF capacity and changes in hospital discharge outcomes, we implemented a first differences regression approach: (1) Δ Y h = Δ O C h + Δ X h + ε h

where ∆ Y h represents the relative change in the discharge outcome at hospital h , while ∆ O C h reflects the relative change in SNF operating capacity for all SNFs in the hospital’s HRR over the same time period. ∆ X h captures changes in the hospital’s admission characteristics as measured by hospital volume and mean predicted length of stay. Changes were calculated annually relative to 2019. Our primary comparison of interest was 2022 compared to 2019, as this was the last year of hospital outcome data available to our study team.

### Additional Analyses

We tested the robustness of our results to alternate specifications including using different (i.e., 15, 30, and 90 day) look-back periods to ascertain a SNF’s maximum resident census and comparing the relationship between changes in SNF capacity and staffing shortages and hospital discharge outcomes in other years (e.g., 2021 or 2023 vs. 2019). We further examined the relationship between SNF-reported staffing shortages and their capacity for new patients with an additional analysis conducted at the facility-week level. We also examined the association of county-level SNF capacity changes with shortages of specific staff types. We explored an alternate measure of capacity changes captured by SNF bed availability (i.e., operating capacity minus current census). Finally, we compared the strength of the association between capacity measures and our outcomes of interest when capacity was estimated using operating capacity vs. using traditional measures based on licensed bed counts. See eAppendix 2 for details.

## Results

The number of licensed SNF beds declined modestly over the study period. In 2019, there were on average 1.60 million nursing home beds. By Q4 2024, the number decreased to 1.56 million, a 2.5% relative decline (Figure 1). Estimated operating capacity, on the other hand, experienced substantial changes during the study period, declining from the 2019 mean of 1.36 million to a low of 1.17 million in Q1 2021 followed by an increase to 1.29 million by Q4 2024. These reductions represented operating capacity declines of 14.0% and 5.0%, respectively. Trends were similar when using alternate lookback periods to measure operating capacity, with longer lookback periods yielding larger operating capacity estimates and shorter periods yielding smaller estimates (eFigure 1).

The number of estimated open beds available for new admissions also declined over the study window (eFigure 2). Following a transient increase in 2021, the number of open beds declined between 2022 and 2024. In 2024, there were on average 3,850 fewer SNF beds available each day for new admissions, 5.6% below the 2019 mean of 68,707 open beds.

Significant geographic variation in changes in SNF operating capacity were found when comparing US counties. Most counties experienced some degree of operating capacity decline in 2024 compared to 2019 and 25% experienced relative declines of 15.1% or more (Figure 2). Some county characteristics varied by the extent of SNF operating capacity declines. For example, counties experiencing the largest declines (i.e., >25% decline) were more likely to be rural (66.8% vs. 49.5%) had lower population densities (80.4, SD=315 vs. 185, SD=452 population per square mile) compared to counties that did not lose SNF capacity (Table 1). Additionally, counties with the largest declines had larger shares of their population who are age 75 and older (mean=7.87%, SD=2.35% vs. mean=6.96%, SD=2.19%) and are White, non-Hispanic race (mean=88.0%, SD=14.1% vs. mean=82.7%, SD=16.8%) compared to counties without declines.

Changes in county-level SNF operating capacity were negatively associated with the frequency of reported staffing shortages (Figure 3). Regression estimates indicated that a 1 percentage point (pp) decline in county SNF capacity was associated with a 0.20 pp increase (95% CI: 0.11, 0.29) in the share of SNF bed-weeks with a reported staff shortage. Changes in SNF capacity were most strongly associated with reported shortages of nurses and aides (eTable 1). The estimated association between operating capacity and staffing shortages were directionally similar in other years (eTable 2) and findings were unchanged when using different lookback periods to estimate operating capacity (eTable 3). In contrast, changes in capacity measured using licensed bed counts were not significantly associated with reported staff shortages (eTable 4). Finally, at the facility-week level, we estimated that increases in SNF reports of recent staffing shortages were associated with reduced SNF patient census (eTable 5).

At the hospital level, changes in operating capacity among SNFs in their catchment area were also significantly correlated with hospital discharge outcomes (Figure 4). After adjusting for changes in hospital volume and case-mix, a 1 pp decrease in nearby SNF capacity was associated with a 0.20 pp (95% CI: 0.14, 0.27) increase in mean hospital length of stay. The estimated relationship was stronger when examining the frequency of extended stays—a 1 pp decrease in SNF capacity was associated with a 1.89 pp (95% CI: 1.28, 2.49) increase in the share of stays lasting 28 days or more. Finaly, reductions in SNF capacity were significantly associated with traveling greater distances to an admitting SNF. A 1pp decline in capacity was linked to a 0.75 pp (95% CI: 0.51, 1.00) increase in the median distance traveled.

Estimated associations were smaller but directionally similar when using changes between 2021 and 2019 (eTable 6) and were unchanged when using alternate lookback periods to estimate operating capacity (eTable 7). The estimated associations were about half as large when using licensed bed counts to measure changes in capacity for mean length of stay and the share of stays lasting 28 days or more analyses; estimates were similar between the two measures of capacity when examining the association with distance traveled. In contrast, only the number of open SNF beds estimated with operating capacity was significantly associated with all of the hospital discharge outcomes (eTable 8).

## Discussion

Despite modest declines in the number of licensed SNF beds following the Covid-19 pandemic, the estimated number of beds in actual operation meaningfully declined. Our estimates indicate that national SNF capacity declined by as much as 14% in Q1 of 2021 and remained 5% below 2019 levels by the end of 2024. Findings also suggest that the US nursing home industry is operating with less slack in the system, as evidenced by a nearly 6% decline in the number of open beds that were available for new admissions in 2024 relative to 2019. These reductions in SNF capacity were not evenly distributed across the country. More than a quarter of counties experienced declines of 15% or more in 2024, and rural counties were at greater risk for experiencing the largest capacity declines. Our estimates indicate that 14% of rural counties had declines in operating capacity of 25% or more, compared with just 9% of suburban counties and 6% of urban counties

The current study is unable to separate the extent to which observed declines in SNF capacity are the result of supply-side constraints (e.g., staffing shortages that necessitate operating fewer SNF beds) or reductions in the demand for SNF beds. However, available evidence suggests that reductions in SNF capacity are unlikely to be caused exclusively by fewer patients seeking SNF care. For instance, hospital volume, a key source of SNF referrals, appears to have returned to pre-pandemic levels.34 Our results also demonstrate a strong correlation between the frequency of reported staffing shortages and SNF capacity declines both at the county level and within individual facilities, consistent with industry and media reports that difficulties hiring and retaining staff were driving market contraction.11,17

The study results are also consistent with reports of demand for SNF beds exceeding available capacity, resulting in hospital bottlenecks and patients being forced to use SNFs further from their preferred location.18,35,36 Specifically, this study demonstrates a strong association between reductions in nearby SNF capacity and increases in hospitals’ mean length of stay, share of stays lasting 28 days or more, and distance traveled to admitting SNFs. Further research is needed to quantify the precise causes of SNF capacity changes, but continued monitoring is warranted to ensure that an aging population can access the post-acute and long-term care services SNFs provide.

Our findings highlight the need to expand measures of SNF market supply beyond simple counts of physical capacity (i.e., the number of licensed beds) to account for the fact that other resources, such as staffing, supplies, or specialized equipment, may be the limiting factors that determine the actual capacity available to patients. For instance, we found a strong negative relationship between SNF-reported staffing shortages and our measure of estimated operating capacity, but not with capacity measures calculated using licensed bed counts. During the pandemic, the US Department of Health and Human Services required hospitals to report, weekly, the number of staffed beds in operation to address these issues.37 Similar efforts, or measures like the ones used in the current study to infer operating capacity, may be needed provide a more complete picture of health system availability.

This study has additional limitations. First, we rely on a self-reported measure of staffing shortages which may be subject to bias and measurement error. Second, the estimated associations between operating capacity and reported staffing shortages and hospital discharge outcomes are not causal and should therefore be interpreted with caution. Third, our study period is marked by several large-scale changes that may have affected SNF use patterns, including Medicare payment reform via the Patient Driven Payment Model, for which we are unable to fully account.38 Finally, this study is unable to characterize the extent to which changes in SNF use have been replaced by alternative sources of care, including home health care, assisted living communities, or discharges to home without care.

In conclusion, US SNF operating capacity has declined since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic and simple counts of licensed beds understate these reductions. There was significant geographic variation in the extent of SNF capacity declines, and areas with greater losses of SNF capacity experienced more frequent reports of SNF staff shortages and increases in delayed hospital discharges. These results demonstrate the value of readily available, but more sophisticated, measures of SNF operating capacity to understand the changing market for post-acute care. Findings also raise concerns that current and future SNF capacity may not meet the needs of an aging US population, particularly in rural areas.
